We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained significant interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs contrastive learning objectives using original data, while its subsequent step employs a pre-trained model to reduce dimensions. We developed three distinct contrastive learning frameworks and found that our framework outperforms other contrastive learning methods in unsupervised features extraction, and even achieves this in reduced dimensions with pre-trained models. When applying the framework to supervised feature extraction, it demonstrates that the framework surpasses other contrastive learning methods and even traditional contrastive learning in both classification performance and dimensionality. Numerical results demonstrate that our contrastive learning framework excels in unsupervised feature extraction, while the framework applied to supervised feature extraction produces superior performance in classification performance and dimensionality.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework of intricate, locally transitive graphs defined in a preceding study, which demonstrated that all twisted wreath quotient structures must be accompanied by a Fulkerson socle of type A.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each level of every variable. To address this issue, we developed an innovative gradient-based algorithm that results in a novel group lasso variant called GRS. This algorithm produces desirable theoretical properties, such as stability, curvature control, and sparse solutions. To make GR scalable to large datasets, we created two novel variants called GRS-sh and GRS-d. Our numerical experiments show that GRS outperforms existing methods like dummy coding, one-hot encoding, and another group lasso variant in terms of solution accuracy and variable selection.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous tasks, but they lack the ability to incorporate structured knowledge, such as graphs and tables, which are commonly used in machine learning algorithms to produce models with an understanding of the world. While pre-trained models can incorporate knowledge through natural language and artificial interventions, each method has distinct limitations, notably in its dependence on supplementary training data and its inflexibility with dynamic knowledge, respectively. This work introduces a new framework called SKILL that utilizes structured knowledge, specifically a simplified table, of another model's learning process as a means to transfer knowledge. When integrated using a simple prompt, we observe that SKILL enables the model to effectively absorb structured knowledge without the need for additional training, thus facilitating an open-ended application domain. Experimental results show that it can also be employed to enhance the performance of a model on inductive reasoning, particularly in scenarios with an intersectional bias.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain and mitigate memory constraints for training large networks, a new model called DPCRN for single-channel speech enhancement is proposed. This model is based on a dual-path convolutional neural network architecture, which comprises two distinct networks: a small memory network with limited convolutional layers and a key point network with a larger capacity. Both networks are composed of dilated convolution modules and traditional convolution blocks and they are connected through a knowledge distillation process. We evaluate the DPCRN model against competing models using widely accepted speech intelligibility and quality metrics, showing that it consistently outperforms them and achieves 12.5% less parameters and 25% less computation compared to the CRN model.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns of convection over a wide range of driving forces, accurately estimating the associated heat transfer scaling across six orders of magnitude.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of 1.45 million socially positive and negatively framed
tweets, which served as input for an emotion-based Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to
analyze and rank the sentiment of new tweets. We evaluated our R Python LSTM network's
performance against other methods, demonstrating that our model outperformed baseline
approaches.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances.

360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. These subtitles, which
refer to important elements within the video and are typically located in a
prominent position, can significantly influence where users direct their
attention. As such, we introduce a new Ngram-driven subtitle element within a
combined random forest model to capitalize on the informative value of video
subtitles. Experimental validation shows that our model can enhance the
accuracy of predicting a user's viewport in 360-degree tourism videos when
processing such content.

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, a framework was developed to optimize the bond dimensions for a specific condition, and the implications of these objects in the context of quantum thermodynamics and information theories were also explored.

We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how non-linear small-x saturation impacts shift the Borel plane's initial IR pole from $2/\beta_2$ to $1/\beta_2$, thereby changing the estimated uncertainty to approximately $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^2$ instead of $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^4$.

Researchers are focusing on extremely thin alloys made of rare earth and transition metals, with controlled composition and unique magnetic properties, to create advanced photonic applications that operate rapidly. Despite the potential, it is very difficult to achieve small scale dimensions, which are essential for scaling down devices, while maintaining the necessary functionality and maintaining the unique magnetic properties. This study demonstrates a breakthrough by integrating minute amounts of ferrimagnetic alloys within a gold nanoarray to create a highly complex crystal that reacts differently to light and controlled magnetic fields, resulting in clear and adjustable features in the spectral patterns. This discovery enables the development of precise light-sensing tools and provides a foundation for innovative technology that could manipulate magnetic properties with light in rare earth and transition metal alloys.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage and privacy concerns. This study introduces decision-based knowledge distillation, a technique that allows a student model to be trained on the outputs of a network's classifier without needing access to the original data or parameters, even when only binary classification results are available. Uniquely, our approach can distill knowledge from a network that was never trained to distinguish between its classification categories, simply by learning from whether it classifies inputs correctly or not. This is achieved using a pair of innovations: mask-based label generation and a reweighted cross-entropy loss function, both designed to accelerate the student model's performance. When applied to multiple black-box scenarios, our method outperforms an alternative approach, demonstrating its effectiveness in leveraging a network without trained supervision.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is $3.48 \times 10^{-4}$, with an uncertainty of $\pm 0.18 \times 10^{-4}$, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is $0.99 \times 10^{-4}$, with an uncertainty of $\pm 0.28 \times 10^{-4}$.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, which can be obtained through character theory. Once the lattice of submodules is determined, we can identify all modules that lie within an interval of this lattice, providing a more comprehensive understanding of their lattice structure.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polar codes. The proposed metric function performs computations in parallel and compares the relative positions of cumulative erasure probabilities to determine the outcome. Our simulation results demonstrate a remarkable improvement in performance on average, which varies from 13.2 percent for short codes to 3.5 percent for 10k-long codes, with the same codewords under AWPNC conditions and PAC decoding, at reduced computations. The proposed metric function also exhibits scalability, with improvements of 1.3 to 2.0 times, depending on code length.

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. Furthermore, a notable improvement can be observed when the action space is reduced without changing the vocabulary, as validated by multiple metrics including BLEU scores, semantic similarity and human assessment. Our research discovered that initializing the final fully connected layer with a layer that generalizes action similarities resulted in substantial RL performance gains, averaging 1.5 BLEU points improvement.

The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating 
because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces and the characteristics of the 
environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous, two-way 
flow of information between the open system and the surrounding environment.

We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute substantially to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by Cheoll and Thomas in base p >= 2, but this changes when 0 < p < 2, where only finite or co-finite subsets are recognisable. The most notable part of our work occurs when numbers are composed of rational length words, where we establish that subsets defined by simultaneous base p/q systems are not generally recognisable, but provide a positive answer when the base systems are related, including the case for identical base systems p/q.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the paper outlining the MongoDB sharded cluster transaction protocol, particularly the coordinator's actions, lacks clarity and does not reflect the current version of the database. To address this shortcoming, we examined the protocol in detail, using Coq to represent the document structure and state of MongoDB, and verified the transactional consistency of all three types of deployments. While doing so, we also confirmed and formalized the transaction protocol for sharded cluster deployments.

Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three via a combinatorial interpretation related to the inverse of the Kostka matrix from Egecioglu-Remmel (1990). This analysis shows the positivity of specific coefficients and confirms $e$-positivity for an expanded class of these functions, beyond a particular instance explored in Cho-Huh (2019).

Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 90 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 34 Watts per square meter, and shows a clear pattern of being higher during some close approaches compared to others. This fluctuation is closely related to variations in proton speed close to the solar center. Notably, the energy flux that could be sent toward the solar wind near the inner edge of our solar system is sometimes close to as high as 1000 Watts per square meter in some specific time periods, and this study is also connected to another investigation that analyzed the same data in relation to the interaction between the solar wind and radiation fields.

Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance exceeding baseline levels by 11 and 14% in two respective scenarios.

Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is reconstructed via the $D_s^{-}$ decay sequence into $K^-K^+\pi^-$, following $D_s^{*-}$ decay into $D_s^{-}\gamma$. The resulting rate is fit with CLN and BGL form factor parametrisations to derive key parameters for both models.

A recent paper provides an analysis of advancements made in categorizing monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potential properties. A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen in mathematical physics and random matrix theories. This class of quadratic potentials displays oscillatory behavior near the origin and we establish an explicit condition to determine non-singularity, including an assessment of localization with respect to polynomial index and the location of zeros within the complex plane. Furthermore, one-dimensional Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics reveals that non-singular potentials arise from combining the harmonic oscillator with polynomial versions of Heisenberg's ladder operators, effectively encapsulating generalized Hermite polynomials. This approach leads to an analog of the Askey-Gaudin identity for the Heisenberg algebra, offering an alternative proof of the Askey-Gaudin and original Gaudin identities for the zeros of Hermite and Racah polynomials, respectively, as well as an analog of the Geronimo-Van Iersel-Weiss identity for the location of zeros of Hermite polynomials.

A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures.

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve step size, and an adjustment factor. Consequently, this formulation enables rapidly and accurately calculating the expected unit hedging cost for various market conditions. Additionally, Monte Carlo simulations are presented to derive a explicit relationship between the expected unit hedging cost and the process driving the options' underlying assets, the option maturity, strike price, volatility, the process driving the options' underlying assets maturity, and the delta-hedging frequency. The efficiency of the proposed method is demonstrated by comparing it to the standard Monte Carlo computation of the expected unit hedging cost for multiple scenarios.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code.

This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessates sophisticated and sensitive experiments that operate in close proximity to the sources they are measuring. As a result, these instruments and their associated electronics can generate significant disturbances and systematic effects that can mimic the signal of the cosmic microwave background and are known to act on a large scale in the sky. Since they can influence the analysis of the data on an extensive level, it is crucial to model them accurately when planning and analyzing experiments. The s4cmb software is designed to do just that, starting with the simulation of a generic detector's response to the cosmic microwave background, including the distortion and smearing of sensitive measurements. The code is further adaptable to model the specific instrumental and electronic effects produced by the experiments mentioned in the research paper. The usefulness of s4cmb is demonstrated in analyzing the data collected by the ACT and S4 experiments.

In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover modifications to the task that enhance the model's ability to capture such dependencies. However, we also note limitations, such as the difficulty in distinguishing the influence of syntactic dependencies from other factors and the difficulty in linearly adding the model's performance gains.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods frequently change, making it imperative to create a novel architecture that can effectively distinguish between real videos and deepfakes across a variety of methods without requiring retraining. In this paper, we present a new network called the MD-CSDNetwork, which incorporates multiple feature domains and employs a dynamically adjusted cross-stitched mechanism to effectively distinguish between real videos and deepfakes. In contrast to using separate feature domains, which has been demonstrated to be computationally inefficient, the MD-CSDNetwork fuses the domains using a dynamic mechanism, requiring significantly fewer parameters and offering improved robustness. Experiments conducted using the Deepfake Detection Challenge (FACCE) and two other multi-method datasets confirm that the MD-CSDNetwork outperforms existing techniques in terms of accuracy, with particularly notable results when using the "grasped" feature domain, which achieves F-scores of 0.903, 0.935, and 0.908 respectively.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initial two problems, which it found particularly engaging.

Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants.

We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL022 which exhibited an unusual movement pattern. We calculated their metal composition and ages as varying significantly across the sample clusters which is consistent with previous research. We calculated the average metal composition and age for the sample clusters and found they differed from the VVV-CL022 cluster. We have added the 19 proposed clusters to the galaxy's globular cluster catalog while designating VVV-CL022 with an unusual movement pattern, VVV-CL045 with a very low

In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for an accurate representation of power-law behaviors in systems. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that utilize diverse types of tensors, allowing these networks to successfully capture the characteristics of power-law behaviors while adhering to the principle of efficient calculation. A concrete example of such a network has also been developed - one that closely resembles the holographic HaPPY pentagon code under the assumption that certain system parameters can be set to a specific small range.

Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determining their effectiveness in predicting
future events at various stages of the process. Our experiments reveal that
deep learning models provide more accurate predictions than conventional methods,
however, their performance fluctuates when trying to predict events at different
stages of the process. Unfortunately, due to the nature of process data, it is
challenging to establish causal connections or derive generalizable patterns from
our results. To address this limitation, we statistically analyze our findings
to create stage-specific predictions for a specific process instance. Our data
shows that future events within the process are not uniform and vary depending
on the current stage of the process instance. Ultimately, our research contributes
to replacing parts of existing process management systems with deep learning models
to predict process events more accurately. Our source code is available online
at https://github.com/itsm404/process-event-prediction-using-deep-learning.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation exists in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare models to assess the feasibility of using a radiative electron beam model. However, such a model fails to explain the strength of the Balmer jump, the structure of the Lyman series, and the Balmer $\alpha$ line wing broadening

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, I introduced a unique smoothing technique tailored to limited smoothness frameworks to limit the impact of such manipulations limited by the same constraints. I demonstrated the unique technique's viability by comparing it to generalizable smoothing alternatives in performance on real-world experiments using diverse datasets and results show 20 to 40 percent boost in performance on stretching and rotation transformations on real-world data and 10 to 30 percent on other common distortions.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia.

Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models use encounter probability functions to characterize an animals' space and resource selection patterns.  Although SSCR models have been shown to provide precise population estimates, their application to animals that can be located with high-precision gear, such as GPS or radio transmitters, is not well-suited.  Researchers using these models are advised to exclude the spatial information from their analyses.  However, integrating these models could allow for the estimation of space and resource selection at the population level for certain animals captured with precise location gear, provided specific conditions are met.  This paper provides a framework for conducting such an analysis and presents the associated theory, simulation studies to illustrate potential pitfalls, and a case-study that demonstrates a practical application.

The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J. Willard Gibbs, and P. and T. Guggenheimer, with varying levels of success. The researchers are unable to find a universal method to determine an unbiased, objective way in which to define or express one of the two incompatible parameters that were used in previous works. Thus, they are unable to conclude with certainty which of these parameters provide the most efficient and reliable framework within which to establish, generalize, and expand upon existing, highly successful mathematical techniques.

The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software. We geographically depict the relationship between these two methodologies' features and characteristics. In particular, we focus on a specific approach that combines geometry, program analysis, and testing to guarantee software that meets certain specifications. We isolate and discuss the elements of geometric-based analysis, testing, and verification before presenting a detailed report on recent research that combines all three approaches to ensure software reliability.

Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$ or $D_l$. Let $K$ be a field whose characteristic is not $2$. Let $\delta$ be the maximal root in the root system $\Phi$ and define the set $\Phi_0$ as consisting of the roots $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ for which $\alpha$ is orthogonal to $\delta$. The group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$ is then described as acting on the set containing elements of the form $e_\alpha$, with the condition that the angle between $\alpha$ and $\delta$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's total number of nodes, $N$, in an environment with malicious actors who can arbitrarily interfere with node interactions. Our analysis begins with a simplified problem where nodes can't directly learn about each other's identities but can infer a lower bound on $N$. We establish that, in 2 rounds of ROST protocol exchanges, the estimation lower bound can be at best $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{f}{k}\log N\log^2\kappa\kappa'\})$, where $f$ is the number of malicious nodes, $k$ is the average connection degree, and $\kappa,\kappa'$ reflect the sparse network's structure. Next, we provide an algorithm to get both lower and upper estimates of $N$ in the more complex scenario. Under the same cost parameters, we prove that the difference between the upper and lower estimates in 2 rounds can be no more than $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{f}{k}\log N\log^3\kappa\kappa'\})$. Notably, in cases with no malicious nodes, our results significantly improve on previous estimates by a factor of $\sqrt{\log \kappa\kappa'}$. Since network estimation forms the foundation for various distributed protocols aiming to operate efficiently on unknown networks, our findings offer a theoretical basis for developing robust, scale-aware distributed systems that can withstand malicious interference.

Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study presents a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or leaving the capacity of
road segments unconstrained.
The method utilizes simple statistical measures, specifically empirical
distributions, and involves minimal computational effort, enabling
implementation on various types of vehicles.
To test the method's performance, two different scenarios were simulated:
estimating local queues based on vehicle position and position changes to
estimate queue lengths at fixed points.
The results show that this nonparametric model provides a reliable
short-term traffic state estimation, thus facilitating more informed
decisions.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of test cases, including non-universal field configurations and spacetimes containing multiple black holes with spinal maximal slicing conditions.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents the first direct measurement of the anomalous Nernst effect in an antiferromagnetic antiperovskite material, specifically an antiperovskite variant known as $ \text{Mn}_3 \text{NiN} $. By carefully analyzing our data and considering the orientation of the material's spiral magnetic structure, we were able to extract the anomalous Nernst coefficient and find it comparable to values reported for other antiferromagnetic materials. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of investigating the anomalous Nernst effect in antiperovskites and pave the way for potential applications based on these materials in generating thermoelectric voltages in antiferromagnetic materials.

Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on accelerating experiments and data collection, which in turn require sophisticated, large-scale facilities like synchrotron light sources. To quickly process vast amounts of data generated during these experiments, machine learning models are proving to be an essential tool. This report will highlight recent achievements in utilizing machine learning to enhance the efficiency of such experiments. Specifically, it will highlight how supervised learning can streamline post-data processing tasks by replacing linear regression methods. Moreover, it will highlight how reinforcement learning can optimize experimental processes and increase data quality. To illustrate these points, the report will draw on real-world cases from the Potts Group's research at the Beamline 11.0.1 of the Advanced Light Source.
